name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q24 - Strongest Bronsted base among cyclic amines

questiontext.text: Among the following amines, the strongest Brönsted base is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four amine structures are evaluated for Brönsted basicity:
Aniline (an aromatic amine with \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\) attached to a benzene ring), ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)), pyrrole (a five-membered heteroaromatic ring containing an \(\mathrm{NH}\) group), and pyrrolidine (a saturated five-membered secondary cyclic amine).

Step 2: Assumptions and Structural Interpretation
A Brönsted base functions as a proton acceptor. Basicity is determined by the availability and electron density of the unshared electron pair on the nitrogen atom and the relative stability of the resulting conjugate acid.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Aliphatic secondary amines are substantially more basic than ammonia and aromatic amines. If the nitrogen lone pair participates in aromatic delocalization (aromatic sextet), it is largely unavailable for protonation, dramatically reducing basicity. Conversely, in a saturated alicyclic amine, electron-releasing inductive (\(+I\)) effects of adjacent methylene groups increase the electron density on nitrogen without any resonance delocalization.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working and Comparison
In pyrrolidine, the ring is fully saturated and the lone pair on nitrogen resides in an \(sp^3\) orbital, localized and enriched by the \(+I\) inductive effect of two alkyl ring residues, giving a \(pK_b\) of approximately \(2.7\).
In ammonia, no alkyl groups are present to provide \(+I\) stabilization (\(pK_b \approx 4.75\)).
In aniline, the lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring through resonance across five canonical structures (\(pK_b \approx 9.4\)).
In pyrrole, the nitrogen lone pair is an essential part of the aromatic \(\pi\)-sextet (\(6\pi\) electrons). Protonation at nitrogen disrupts aromaticity, making pyrrole an extremely weak base (\(pK_b \approx 13.6\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Pyrrolidine possesses the highest electron density on nitrogen and is the strongest Brönsted base.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q25 - Decreasing order of basic strength of species

questiontext.text:
The correct decreasing order of basic strength of the following species is

\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}, \mathrm{NH}_3, \mathrm{OH}^-, \mathrm{NH}_2^-\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Brönsted basicity reflects proton-accepting ability. Negatively charged conjugate bases (anions) are fundamentally stronger bases than their corresponding neutral conjugate acids because of greater electron density and charge attraction toward protons. Furthermore, across a period in the periodic table, basicity of isoelectronic species decreases with increasing electronegativity of the central atom.

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Comparing anionic species (\(\mathrm{NH}_2^-\) versus \(\mathrm{OH}^-\)): Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen (electronegativity of \(\mathrm{N} \approx 3.0\) versus \(\mathrm{O} \approx 3.5\)). Consequently, the amide ion (\(\mathrm{NH}_2^-\)) holds its negative charge less tightly and donates its electron pair to a proton more readily than the hydroxide ion (\(\mathrm{OH}^-\)), making \(\mathrm{NH}_2^- > \mathrm{OH}^-\).
Comparing neutral species (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\) versus \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)): By the same electronegativity difference, nitrogen donates its lone pair more readily than oxygen, making ammonia a stronger base than water (\(\mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)).
Because anions have significantly higher basic strength than neutral molecules, the overall basicity sequence becomes: \[\mathrm{NH}_2^- > \mathrm{OH}^- > \mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct decreasing order of basic strength is \(\mathrm{NH}_2^- > \mathrm{OH}^- > \mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q26 - Identification of most volatile organic compound

questiontext.text:
Which of the following should be most volatile?

(I) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{NH}_2\)
(II) \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{N}\)
(III) \(\begin{array}{c} \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2 \\ | \\ \mathrm{CH}_3 \end{array} > \mathrm{NH}\)
(IV) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Volatility is inversely proportional to boiling point; a substance with weaker intermolecular forces exhibits a lower boiling point and greater volatility at a given temperature.

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Compound (I) is propan-1-amine, a primary amine possessing two \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds capable of forming strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, giving it a relatively high boiling point (\(\approx 48^\circ\mathrm{C}\)).
Compound (III) is ethylmethylamine, a secondary amine with one \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}\) bond that forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds, giving a boiling point of \(\approx 36^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
Compound (II) is trimethylamine, a tertiary amine lacking \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds. It cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with itself, but its polar \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{N}\) bonds participate in dipole–dipole interactions (boiling point \(\approx 3^\circ\mathrm{C}\)).
Compound (IV) is propane, an almost non-polar hydrocarbon whose molecules interact only via very weak London dispersion forces (boiling point \(\approx -42^\circ\mathrm{C}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because it experiences only weak dispersion forces without dipole–dipole or hydrogen bonding interactions, propane (IV) has the lowest boiling point and is the most volatile compound.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q27 - Preparation of amines and carbon chain retention

questiontext.text: Which of the following methods of preparation of amines will give same number of carbon atoms in the chain of amines as in the reactant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In organic amine synthesis, reactions can proceed with retention of the carbon chain length, ascent of the series (lengthening the chain, as via nitrile reduction), or descent of the series (shortening the chain, as in degradation reactions).

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Reaction of an amide with \(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\) followed by water reduces \(-\mathrm{CONH}_2\) directly to \(-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{NH}_2\), preserving the exact number of carbon atoms.
Heating an alkyl halide with potassium phthalimide followed by hydrolysis (Gabriel synthesis) replaces the halogen with an amino group without modifying the alkyl chain length.
In contrast, treatment of an amide with bromine in aqueous sodium hydroxide is the Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction: \[\mathrm{R-CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\] Here, the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate, producing a primary amine containing one carbon atom fewer than the starting amide (the question in standard examination banks targets this degradation method).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Treatment of an amide with bromine in aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide is the degradation method associated with a change in the carbon skeleton (yielding one carbon atom less).

answer.text: Reaction of amide with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) followed by treatment with water.
Heating alkylhalide with potassium salt of phthalimide followed by hydrolysis.
Treatment of amide with bromine in aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q28 - Compounds not prepared by Sandmeyer reaction

questiontext.text: Which of the following cannot be prepared by Sandmeyer's reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sandmeyer's reaction specifically refers to the introduction of chloro, bromo, or cyano groups into a benzene ring by reacting a freshly prepared arenediazonium salt with cuprous salts dissolved in the corresponding halogen acid (\(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}/\mathrm{HCl}\) or \(\mathrm{Cu_2Br_2}/\mathrm{HBr}\)).

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Chlorobenzene and bromobenzene are prepared via Sandmeyer's reaction using \(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}/\mathrm{HCl}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu_2Br_2}/\mathrm{HBr}\) respectively.
Iodobenzene does not require a cuprous salt; it is simply prepared by shaking the arenediazonium salt solution with potassium iodide (\(\mathrm{KI}\)).
Fluorobenzene is prepared by the Balz–Schiemann reaction, where diazonium fluoroborate (\(\mathrm{ArN_2^+BF_4^-}\)) is precipitated and thermally decomposed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Neither iodobenzene nor fluorobenzene can be prepared by Sandmeyer's reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q29 - Reagents for reducing nitrobenzene to aniline

questiontext.text: Reduction of nitrobenzene by which of the following reagent gives aniline?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nitrobenzene (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2}\)) can be reduced directly to primary aromatic amine (aniline, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)) using active reducing metals in acidic medium or through catalytic hydrogenation over transition metal catalysts.

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Tin in concentrated hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{Sn/HCl}\)) generates nascent hydrogen that reduces nitrobenzene smoothly to aniline.
Iron scrap in hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{Fe/HCl}\)) is an efficient reagent that reduces nitrobenzene to aniline, requiring only catalytic amounts of acid due to hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{FeCl}_2\).
Hydrogen gas over palladium catalyst (\(\mathrm{H_2}\text{-Pd}\)) performs catalytic hydrogenation of the nitro group cleanly into an amino group.
Reduction of nitrobenzene using tin in alkaline medium (\(\mathrm{Sn}/\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{OH}\)) does not yield aniline, giving bimolecular intermediate reduction products instead.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Sn/HCl}\), \(\mathrm{Fe/HCl}\), and \(\mathrm{H}_2\text{-Pd}\) reduce nitrobenzene to aniline.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q30 - Species involved in the carbylamine test

questiontext.text: Which of the following species are involved in the carbylamine test?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The carbylamine reaction (isocyanide test) is a selective test for primary aliphatic and aromatic amines. Heating a primary amine with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide produces an extremely foul-smelling isocyanide (carbylamine).

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
The chemical reaction is given by: \[\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\] Chloroform (\(\mathrm{CHCl}_3\)) serves as the key reagent that generates the reactive intermediate dichlorocarbene (\(:\!\mathrm{CCl}_2\)), and the alkyl isocyanide (\(\mathrm{R-NC}\)) is the characteristic foul-smelling product formed.
Phosgene (\(\mathrm{COCl}_2\)) and nitrous acid (\(\mathrm{NaNO}_2 + \mathrm{HCl}\)) are not part of the carbylamine reaction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{R-NC}\) and \(\mathrm{CHCl}_3\) are the species involved in the carbylamine test.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q31 - Conversion of benzenediazonium chloride to benzene

questiontext.text: The reagents that can be used to convert benzenediazonium chloride to benzene are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The replacement of the diazonium group (\(-\mathrm{N}_2^+\)) by hydrogen (deamination to parent arene) is achieved by treating an arenediazonium salt with mild reducing agents.

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\), phosphinic acid) in the presence of water reduces benzenediazonium chloride to benzene with simultaneous evolution of nitrogen, while being oxidized to phosphorous acid: \[\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{N}_2^+\mathrm{Cl}^- + \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6 + \mathrm{N}_2 + \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3 + \mathrm{HCl}\]
Ethanol (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH}\)) also reduces benzenediazonium chloride to benzene while being oxidized to ethanal: \[\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{N}_2^+\mathrm{Cl}^- + \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6 + \mathrm{N}_2 + \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\]
\(\mathrm{SnCl}_2/\mathrm{HCl}\) reduces diazonium salts to phenylhydrazine rather than benzene, and \(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\) is not used for this selective deamination.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) are the reagents that convert benzenediazonium chloride to benzene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q32 - Products of electrophilic bromination of acetanilide

questiontext.text: The product of the following reaction is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Acetanilide (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3}\)) is treated with bromine in ethanoic acid (\(\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)). Four potential brominated products are shown: 4-bromoacetanilide (para isomer), 2-bromoacetanilide (ortho isomer), 3-bromoacetanilide (meta isomer), and 2,4,6-tribromoacetanilide.

Step 2: Assumptions and Structural Interpretation
The reaction is an electrophilic aromatic substitution on a mono-substituted benzene derivative where the directing group is an acetamido group (\(-\mathrm{NHCOCH}_3\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The \(-\mathrm{NHCOCH}_3\) group has an unshared electron pair on nitrogen that can be donated to the benzene ring via resonance, activating the ring and directing incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions. However, the bulky acetylamino group sterically hinders attack at the ortho position.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working and Comparison
Bromination in acetic acid occurs under controlled, mild conditions without polybromination.
Electrophilic attack by \(\mathrm{Br}^+\) at the less sterically hindered para position yields 4-bromoacetanilide as the predominant major product.
Electrophilic attack at the ortho position also takes place to a minor extent, yielding 2-bromoacetanilide.
Meta substitution is disfavored because the arenium intermediate lacks resonance stabilization by the nitrogen lone pair, and 2,4,6-tribromination only occurs with activated free aniline, not protected acetanilide.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both 4-bromoacetanilide and 2-bromoacetanilide are the products formed in the reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q33 - Arenium ions in electrophilic bromination of aniline

questiontext.text: Arenium ion involved in the bromination of aniline is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four arenium ion (\(\sigma\)-complex) canonical structures representing electrophilic attack of \(\mathrm{Br}^+\) on aniline are depicted: two corresponding to ortho attack (one with positive charge in the ring and one with an exocyclic double bond to a positively charged nitrogen), one corresponding to para attack with an exocyclic double bond to \(\mathrm{NH}_2^+\), and one representing meta attack.

Step 2: Assumptions and Structural Interpretation
Electrophilic aromatic substitution proceeds via attack of \(\mathrm{Br}^+\) on the benzene ring, forming an arenium cation (Wheland complex) stabilized by delocalization across the ring carbons and onto the nitrogen atom.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The amino group (\(-\mathrm{NH}_2\)) is an exceptionally powerful activating and ortho/para-directing group due to its \(+M\) resonance effect. The arenium intermediates formed during ortho and para attack are especially stable because the unshared electron pair of nitrogen can be shared with the ring, forming an additional resonance structure where every second-row atom possesses a complete octet.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working and Comparison
During ortho attack of \(\mathrm{Br}^+\), resonance delocalizes the positive charge to the ring carbons and into the nitrogen atom, generating the resonance forms with positive charge adjacent to the \(sp^3\) carbon and with an exocyclic double bond \(=\!\mathrm{NH}_2^+\).
During para attack of \(\mathrm{Br}^+\), resonance similarly delocalizes the positive charge to nitrogen, giving the quinonoid-type arenium ion with \(=\!\mathrm{NH}_2^+\).
Meta attack does not permit direct octet stabilization by the nitrogen lone pair, and bromination of aniline occurs almost exclusively at the ortho and para positions.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The arenium ions corresponding to ortho and para bromination of aniline are the contributing intermediates involved in the reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q34 - Amines prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis

questiontext.text: Which of the following amines can be prepared by Gabriel synthesis.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is used exclusively for the preparation of primary aliphatic amines. It relies on the nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) of an alkyl halide by the phthalimide anion, followed by hydrolysis to yield a pure primary amine.

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Isobutylamine, \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{NH}_2\), is a primary aliphatic amine derived from isobutyl halide via \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) displacement; it can be prepared by Gabriel synthesis.
2-Phenylethylamine, \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{NH}_2\), contains an aliphatic primary amino group and can be synthesized from 2-phenylethyl halide.
N-methylbenzylamine is a secondary amine; Gabriel synthesis yields exclusively primary amines.
Aniline is an aromatic primary amine. Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion under normal conditions due to resonance strengthening of the carbon–halogen bond.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Isobutyl amine and 2-phenylethylamine can be prepared by Gabriel synthesis.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q35 - Evaluation of organic reactions of amines

questiontext.text: Which of the following reactions are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four chemical transformations are shown:
Reaction (i): Ammonolysis of a primary alkyl chloride with two moles of ammonia yielding a primary amine and ammonium chloride.
Reaction (ii): Treatment of tert-butyl chloride with aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\) shown yielding 2-methylpropene.
Reaction (iii): Dehydrohalogenation of cyclohexyl chloride with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) yielding cyclohexene.
Reaction (iv): Reaction of propan-1-amine with nitrous acid at \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\) shown yielding 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol).

Step 2: Assumptions and Chemical Principles
Primary alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) with excess ammonia to yield primary amines. Secondary and tertiary alkyl halides undergo elimination with strong alcoholic base to form alkenes, whereas aqueous base promotes substitution over elimination for tertiary alkyl halides. Reaction of primary amines with nitrous acid proceeds without adding carbon atoms to the molecular formula.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working and Evaluation
Reaction (i) depicts standard ammonolysis of a primary alkyl halide: \[\mathrm{R-CH_2-Cl} + 2\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-CH_2-NH_2} + \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\] This is a correct and standard synthetic pathway.
Reaction (ii) shows aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\) with tert-butyl chloride giving an alkene; however, aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\) favors nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)) forming tert-butyl alcohol rather than dehydrohalogenation.
Reaction (iii) shows treatment of cyclohexyl chloride with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\), which is a classic \(\beta\)-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) providing cyclohexene cleanly. This reaction is correct.
Reaction (iv) shows a three-carbon amine (propan-1-amine) reacting with \(\mathrm{HNO}_2\) to yield a four-carbon tertiary alcohol (tert-butyl alcohol), which violates the conservation of carbon atoms.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Reactions (i) and (iii) represent chemically correct transformations.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q36 - Reaction conditions for para nitration of aniline

questiontext.text: Under which of the following reaction conditions, aniline gives \(p\)-nitro derivative as the major product?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Direct nitration of aniline with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) leads to extensive oxidation to tarry products and protonation of the amino group to the anilinium ion (\(-\mathrm{NH}_3^+\)), which is strongly meta-directing and yields substantial \(m\)-nitroaniline (\(47\%\)). To obtain the \(p\)-nitro derivative as the predominant product, the activating effect of the \(-NH_2\) group must be protected by acetylation prior to nitration.

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Reacting aniline with acetyl chloride in pyridine or acetic anhydride in pyridine protects the amino group as acetanilide (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3}\)). The lone pair of nitrogen is partially delocalized to the carbonyl oxygen, reducing electron donation to the benzene ring. Subsequent nitration of acetanilide with conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) and conc. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) selectively directs the incoming nitronium ion to the less sterically hindered para position, affording \(p\)-nitroacetanilide as the major product. Subsequent hydrolysis then furnishes \(p\)-nitroaniline.
Treatment with dilute \(\mathrm{HCl}\) or direct treatment with nitrating acid protonates aniline to anilinium ion, yielding meta-nitroaniline as a significant product rather than selective para-mononitration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Protection of aniline using acetyl chloride in pyridine or acetic anhydride in pyridine followed by nitration gives the \(p\)-nitro derivative as the major product.

answer.text: Acetyl chloride/pyridine followed by reaction with conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 +\) conc. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\)
Dil. HCl followed by reaction with conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 +\) conc. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q37 - Identification of electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions

questiontext.text: Which of the following reactions belong to electrophilic aromatic substitution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrophilic aromatic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_EAr}\)) involves the attack of an electrophile on the \(\pi\)-electron system of an aromatic ring, resulting in the substitution of a ring hydrogen atom by the electrophilic moiety.

Step 2: Chemical Evaluation
Bromination of acetanilide involves generation of the electrophile \(\mathrm{Br}^+\), which attacks the aromatic ring of acetanilide to substitute a ring hydrogen atom at the ortho or para position; this is a classic electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction.
Coupling reaction of aryldiazonium salts involves the diazonium cation (\(\mathrm{ArN}_2^+\)) acting as an electrophile that attacks an activated aromatic ring (such as phenol or aniline) at the para position to form an azo compound; this is an electrophilic aromatic substitution.
Diazotisation of aniline involves nucleophilic attack by the amino nitrogen atom of aniline on the nitrosonium ion (\(\mathrm{NO}^+\)), occurring at the exocyclic nitrogen rather than the aromatic ring.
Acylation of aniline involves nucleophilic attack by the amino nitrogen atom on the carbonyl carbon of an acyl chloride or anhydride, which is a nucleophilic acyl substitution on the nitrogen atom.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Bromination of acetanilide and the coupling reaction of aryldiazonium salts are electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions.
